mainTopic: Counting the years of ערלה and רבעי, and whether a partial year counts as a year according to רבי מאיר
overview: This amud ends a ברייתא: the fruit of a young tree stays forbidden until ט״ו בשבט, both in the ערלה years and in the רבעי year. The גמרא asks for the source. רבי יוחנן, also reported in the name of רבי ינאי, points to the extra 'and' in 'ובשנה הרביעית ובשנה החמישית'. This shows that fruit can still be ערלה in the fourth year and still רבעי in the fifth. Next, the גמרא suggests that the planting ברייתא, which requires thirty days before ראש השנה, does not follow רבי מאיר. רבי מאיר holds that one day in a year counts as a whole year. The גמרא proves his view from a ברייתא about the age of a פר, where רבי אלעזר requires thirty days instead. The גמרא answers that רבי מאיר's rule applies only at the end of a count, not at the beginning. רבא then challenges this answer with a קל וחומר from נדה, and his argument continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Fruit stays forbidden until ט״ו בשבט
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by ruling that the fruit of this planting stays forbidden until ט״ו בשבט, for both ערלה and רבעי.
steps.simpleTranslation: The fruit of this planting is forbidden until the fifteenth of Shevat. If it is in its ערלה years, it is ערלה. If it is in its רבעי year, it is רבעי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting a ברייתא. It says that even after the years turn over at ראש השנה (in תשרי), the fruit stays forbidden until ט״ו בשבט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The years of the tree are counted from ראש השנה in תשרי. Even so, the fruit-status of ערלה or רבעי carries on past תשרי until ט״ו בשבט, the new year for trees. The same rule applies to both stages: ערלה, which is fully forbidden, and רבעי, which must be eaten in ירושלים or redeemed.

keyTerms.meaning: a planting; a young tree
fruit of a tree's first three years, which may not be eaten
fourth-year fruit, eaten in ירושלים or redeemed
the 15th of Shevat, the new year for trees

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the tree's years are counted from ט״ו בשבט. The years still turn over at ראש השנה in תשרי. Only the fruit's forbidden status carries on until ט״ו בשבט.

phrases.english: And the fruit of this planting is forbidden
until the fifteenth of Shevat,
if for orlah, it is orlah,
phrases.notes: During the ערלה years, the fruit stays ערלה until ט״ו בשבט.

phrases.english: and if for fourth-year produce, it is fourth-year produce.
phrases.notes: During the fourth year, the fruit stays רבעי until ט״ו בשבט of the fifth year.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפֵירוֹת נְטִיעָה זוֹ אֲסוּרִין עַד חֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר בִּשְׁבָט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends a ברייתא that the גמרא began quoting on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The fruit stays ערלה or רבעי until ט״ו בשבט, even though the tree's year turned over at ראש השנה.

steps.title: What is the source for this rule?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where we learn that the forbidden status goes on until ט״ו בשבט.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we learn these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of the ברייתא's rule. This sets up the next step, where a פסוק is brought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a year ends at ראש השנה. So stretching the ban into שבט needs a source in the תורה. The גמרא wants to find it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these matters learned?

phrases.english: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rule in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The פסוק that teaches the ban continues past ראש השנה until ט״ו בשבט.

steps.title: The source is the extra 'and' in the verse
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא, quoting רבי יוחנן (and some say רבי ינאי), brings the פסוק 'ובשנה הרביעית ובשנה החמישית'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן, and some traced it to רבי ינאי: The פסוק says, 'And in the fourth year... and in the fifth year.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by pointing to the פסוקים about ערלה and רבעי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each new year in the פסוק begins with an extra 'and' (the letter ו). That joins each year to the one before it. This hints that the earlier year's status spills over into the next year.

keyTerms.meaning: and some traced it back to the name of
and in the fourth year

phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said
that Rabbi Yochanan said,
and some traced it to the name of Rabbi Yannai,
the verse says: "And in the fourth year"
"and in the fifth year."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The extra 'and' in 'ובשנה הרביעית ובשנה החמישית' joins each year to the year before it.

steps.title: Fruit can still be ערלה in the fourth year, and still רבעי in the fifth
steps.stepSummary: The derivation is explained: sometimes the tree is in its fourth year but the fruit is still ערלה, and sometimes it is in its fifth year but the fruit is still רבעי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sometimes it is in the fourth year and still forbidden as ערלה. Sometimes it is in the fifth year and still forbidden as רבעי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out what the extra 'and' teaches. Fruit can keep its old status even after the new year has started.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the 'and' is read as an overlap between the years. After ראש השנה of the fourth year, fruit that grew before ט״ו בשבט is still ערלה. The same is true for רבעי in the fifth year. This is the source for the ברייתא in step 1.

keyTerms.meaning: sometimes
and it is still forbidden
because of; under the law of

steps.whatToRemember: The 'and' in 'ובשנה הרביעית ובשנה החמישית' teaches that ערלה reaches into the fourth year, and רבעי reaches into the fifth year, until ט״ו בשבט.

phrases.english: There are times that it is in the fourth year
and still forbidden as orlah,
and there are times that it is in the fifth year
and still forbidden as fourth-year produce.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּעָמִים שֶׁבָּרְבִיעִית וַעֲדַיִין אֲסוּרָה מִשּׁוּם עׇרְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the פסוק in step 3 proves the rule.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The overlap means ערלה continues into the fourth year and רבעי into the fifth year.

steps.title: Does this teaching disagree with רבי מאיר?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the ברייתא may not follow רבי מאיר, who holds that one day in a year counts as a whole year.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this does not follow רבי מאיר? For רבי מאיר said that one day in a year counts as a year.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a problem. The ברייתא's way of counting may clash with רבי מאיר's view that part of a year counts as a full year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The planting ברייתא (from the previous amud) says a tree must be planted thirty days before ראש השנה for that year to count as its first year. רבי מאיר counts even one day of a year as a whole year, so for him one day before ראש השנה should be enough. 'לימא' marks a suggestion that the גמרא may later reject.

keyTerms.meaning: shall we say? (a suggestion that may be rejected)
that it does not follow the opinion of
one day in a year counts as a year

steps.confusionAlert: 'לימא' is only a suggestion. The גמרא often goes on to show the teaching can fit that תנא after all.

phrases.english: Let us say that it is not in accordance with Rabbi Meir,
for if it were Rabbi Meir, didn't he say:
one day in a year is considered a year.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns from the source of the rule to whether it fits the view of a תנא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The planting ברייתא's requirement that a tree be planted thirty days before ראש השנה for that year to count.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי מאיר counts even one day of a year as a full year. But the planting ברייתא requires thirty days before ראש השנה for the first year to count. So the ברייתא seems not to follow רבי מאיר.

steps.title: Proof of רבי מאיר's view from the age of a פר
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows רבי מאיר's view: a פר mentioned in the תורה without details is twenty-four months and one day old.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a ברייתא: A פר mentioned in the תורה without details is twenty-four months and one day old. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source showing that רבי מאיר really holds that one day counts as a year.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פר is known by tradition to be three years old. רבי מאיר says that once it is one day into its third year (24 months and one day), it already counts as three years old. That shows that, for him, a single day counts as a full year.

keyTerms.meaning: a bull offered as a קרבן
without details; unspecified

phrases.english: As it is taught: a bull mentioned in the Torah without specification

phrases.aramaic: בֶּן עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה חֹדֶשׁ וְיוֹם אֶחָד.
phrases.english: is twenty-four months and one day old.
These are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the claim in step 5 about רבי מאיר's view.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי מאיר holds one day in a year counts as a whole year.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא that a פר is 24 months and one day old, according to רבי מאיר.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר requires thirty extra days for a פר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues with רבי אלעזר, who says a פר must be twenty-four months and thirty days old.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says: a פר is twenty-four months and thirty days old.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא keeps quoting the same ברייתא it started in step 6. Now we hear the other opinion: רבי אלעזר says a פר must be twenty-four months plus thirty days old.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר said one extra day past two years is enough. רבי אלעזר needs thirty days. So רבי אלעזר holds that thirty days of a year counts as a year, but one day does not. This matches the planting ברייתא, which also needs thirty days.

keyTerms.meaning: Twenty-four months, which is two full years
Thirty days, the minimum amount of a year that counts as a year according to this view

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar says:
[a bull is] twenty-four months old
and thirty days.
phrases.notes: Thirty days into the third year, as opposed to רבי מאיר's one day.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר: בֶּן עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה חֹדֶשׁ וּשְׁלֹשִׁים יוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא and gives the opinion that disagrees with רבי מאיר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A פר is twenty-four months and thirty days old, so thirty days, not one day, of a year counts as a year.

steps.title: רבי מאיר's age rule for עגל, בן בקר, and פר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains רבי מאיר's view: an עגל is in its first year, a בן בקר is in its second, and a פר is in its third. So one day into the third year makes it a פר.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רבי מאיר used to say: wherever the תורה says עגל without details, it means one year old. A בן בקר is two years old. A פר is three years old.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the reason for רבי מאיר's number. A פר is a 'three-year-old,' so as soon as it is one day into its third year, it counts as three.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This proves that רבי מאיר holds one day in a year counts as a whole year. The planting ברייתא needs thirty days, so it seems to follow רבי אלעזר and not רבי מאיר. That is exactly the קשיא raised in step 5.

keyTerms.meaning: Calf, an animal in its first year
Young ox, an animal in its second year
Bull, an animal in its third year
Without specification, mentioned with no age given

steps.confusionAlert: 'בן שלש' does not mean the bull has finished three full years. It means it is IN its third year. That is why two years plus one day is enough for רבי מאיר.

phrases.english: For Rabbi Meir would say:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר עֵגֶל בַּתּוֹרָה סְתָם —
phrases.english: Wherever 'calf' is stated in the Torah without specification —
it is one year old;
'young ox' — it is two years old;
'bull' — it is three years old.
phrases.notes: So once it is one day into its third year, it is a פר.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר עֵגֶל בַּתּוֹרָה סְתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind רבי מאיר's 'twenty-four months and one day' from step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי מאיר holds one day in a year counts as a full year, so the planting ברייתא (thirty days) seems not to follow him.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי מאיר's age scale for עגל, בן בקר, and פר in the ברייתא.

steps.title: רבי מאיר's rule applies only at the end of a count
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the planting ברייתא can still follow רבי מאיר. One day counts as a year only at the 'end' of a count, not at the very beginning.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say the ברייתא follows רבי מאיר. When רבי מאיר said one day in a year counts as a year, that is at the end of the count. But at the beginning of the count, it does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the planting ברייתא. It says the ברייתא does not have to disagree with רבי מאיר, because his rule has a limit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the פר, two full years have already passed, so one more day can count as a third year. With a new planting, there are no full years behind it yet; this is the very first year. רבי מאיר never said one day counts there, so thirty days can be needed even according to him.

keyTerms.meaning: Even if you say, a formula that keeps the original position
Considered a full year
At the end of the count, after full years have already passed
At the beginning of the count, the very first year

steps.whyThisMatters: This limit on רבי מאיר's rule is what רבא now attacks. The rest of the סוגיא depends on whether the end/beginning distinction holds up.

phrases.english: You can even say it follows Rabbi Meir;
when Rabbi Meir said
one day in a year counts as a year —
that is at the end of a year,
phrases.notes: Like the פר, after two full years.

phrases.english: but at the beginning of a year — no.
phrases.notes: Like a new planting, which has no full years behind it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא from steps 5 to 8 by limiting רבי מאיר's rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the planting ברייתא cannot follow רבי מאיר
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a rule (אוקימתא of רבי מאיר's principle)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר counts one day as a year everywhere, so the ברייתא requiring thirty days must disagree with him.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר counts one day only at the end of a count, after full years. At the start of a count, more is needed, so the ברייתא can follow him.

steps.title: רבא's קל וחומר from נדה
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges the answer with a קל וחומר. For a נדה, a little bit at the end of a day counts at the beginning of her count, even though it does not count at the end. So for a year, where one day counts at the end, it should surely count at the beginning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Isn't there a קל וחומר? A נדה: the beginning of a day does not count for her at the end of her count, yet the end of a day does count for her at the beginning of her count. A year, where one day counts at the end —
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the answer from step 9. He builds a קל וחומר from נדה to argue the opposite: if one day counts at the end, it should certainly count at the beginning. This passage stops mid-sentence; the conclusion comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With נדה, the beginning is easier than the end: a few minutes before sunset counts as her first day, but the morning of her seventh day does not finish her count. So 'beginning' is the easier place to count a partial unit. If a year already counts one day at the harder spot, the end, then it should surely count one day at the beginning.

keyTerms.meaning: An argument from a lighter case to a stronger case
A woman in her seven-day period of impurity
Counts for her, is credited as a full day

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two directions. For נדה, the END of a day counts at the BEGINNING of her seven days. But the BEGINNING of a day does NOT count at the END of her seven days, because she waits for nightfall to immerse.

phrases.english: Rava said:
But isn't it an a fortiori argument?
Just as a menstruating woman,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין תְּחִילַּת הַיּוֹם עוֹלָה לָהּ בְּסוֹפָהּ —
phrases.english: for whom the beginning of the day does not count at the end [of her period] —
phrases.notes: On the seventh day she must wait until night to immerse.

phrases.english: yet the end of the day counts for her at the beginning [of her period].
phrases.notes: Bleeding just before sunset makes that day her first day.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁנָה, שֶׁיּוֹם אֶחָד עוֹלֶה לָהּ בְּסוֹפָהּ —
phrases.english: a year, where one day counts at its end —
phrases.notes: The sentence continues on the next amud: surely one day should count at its beginning.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: וְלָאו קַל וָחוֹמֶר הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the end/beginning distinction from step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי מאיר's one-day rule works only at the end of a count, not at the beginning
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר from נדה: the beginning of a count is easier to fill than the end. So if one day counts as a year at the end, it should surely count at the beginning, and the planting ברייתא would again contradict רבי מאיר.
